content: Per diem payments to community health workers were a significant factor in intervention parameters, accounting for 6% of the costs. After this point, cost reductions began to level off. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) assessed the resources required for Reactive Case Detection and Treatment (RACDT) as moderate, with the extent of resources needed depending on the number of index cases. However, no studies were identified that evaluated whether RACDT improved or worsened health equity, leaving the GDG unable to make a judgment on this aspect. Community acceptance of RACDT was high, with refusal rates of 2% or lower, as evidenced by three studies conducted in Namibia, Senegal, and Zambia. In Namibia, initial hesitation or resistance was reported during the pre-trial phase, but community engagement and sensitization efforts appeared to improve participation. Similarly, in Senegal, high participation in RACDT was attributed to advanced community sensitization, follow-up appointments for absent members, and return visits to households on the same or next day. In Zambia, however, challenges included a lack of community confidence in health workers’ ability to address diseases beyond malaria and reluctance to visit health workers for malaria testing. No studies directly addressed healthcare workers’ acceptance of RACDT, but related information from Zambia revealed that community health workers lacked motivation to conduct RACDT. This was partly due to feeling unrecognized for their community service and the absence of financial support or stipends, as they were volunteers. Despite these challenges, the GDG judged RACDT to be probably acceptable to key stakeholders. Seventeen studies, including seven from sub-Saharan Africa and eight from the Asia-Pacific region, provided data on the feasibility and health system considerations of RACDT. The proportion of households reached by RACDT varied geographically, ranging from 49% in Zanzibar to 100% in Jiangsu, China. Timely household reach also varied, from 20% in Zanzibar to 100% in China. Barriers to RACDT implementation were identified at all stages, including low detection and notification of index cases from private health facilities in Cambodia and Zanzibar, which were often missed by RACDT. Engaging the private sector in malaria surveillance was deemed critical, especially in areas where patients frequently use private providers, drug shops, and pharmacies. Within the public health sector, barriers included delayed presentation of malaria patients to health facilities, inadequate preparation of village clinics for surveillance programs, and insufficient human resources and malaria rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). During peak malaria transmission seasons, community health workers were overwhelmed by patient volumes, leading to lower proportions of case investigations. To address these challenges, a study in Zambia suggested increasing the number of community health workers or suspending RACDT during high-transmission seasons. Geographical challenges, such as accessing mountainous terrains, flooded areas, and border regions with mobile populations, also hindered timely follow-up during RACDT interventions. In Zambia, it was recommended that community health workers in flood-prone areas be provided with rain gear and boats. High household density in the Asia-Pacific region posed additional challenges, as did incomplete case investigation forms and the lack of household-level listings of individuals in RACDT areas, which limited follow-up efforts. Imported cases presented a significant challenge for RACDT, as district-level responses alone were insufficient to interrupt transmission when most cases were imported. Stockouts of malaria RDTs, limitations in RDT detection capabilities, and the inability of Plasmodium falciparum-only RDTs to detect other species or low-density infections were also identified as barriers. In Botswana, while malaria microscopy was used as the gold standard for diagnosis, ensuring high-quality slide preparation by health center staff was challenging. The GDG concluded that RACDT was likely feasible to implement, but its success depended on factors such as the availability of G6PD deficiency testing, pharmacovigilance systems, and emergency blood transfusion services for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax infections. Reactive Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) was also considered a potentially effective strategy in areas approaching malaria elimination or post-elimination settings. Reactive IRS involves spraying insecticide in the homes of confirmed malaria cases and their neighbors to prevent onward transmission. Its effectiveness depends on strong passive surveillance systems, timely case investigations, and the ability to determine the likely location of infection. The GDG judged that reactive IRS was probably more cost-effective than proactive IRS in low-transmission settings where cases are clustered. However, the benefits of introducing reactive IRS depend on whether a proactive IRS program is already in place and the characteristics of the local vector and human populations. Reactive IRS was found to reduce malaria prevalence significantly, with high-certainty evidence, but had little to no effect on the incidence of clinical malaria. It also resulted in minimal differences in adverse events compared to proactive IRS. Community acceptance of reactive IRS was high, with refusal rates below 1% when advance notification was provided. Participants generally viewed reactive IRS as a useful malaria prevention tool, citing its effectiveness in reducing mosquitoes and flies. The GDG noted that reactive IRS would likely be more accepted by households than proactive IRS, as residents would understand its purpose in response to a detected malaria case nearby. The GDG emphasized the importance of malaria surveillance as a key intervention in all malaria-endemic countries and those at risk of re-establishing transmission. Surveillance systems should enable program managers to identify high-risk areas, assess intervention impacts, detect and respond to epidemics, and monitor progress toward malaria elimination. Subnational stratification of malaria risk was recommended to tailor interventions to specific populations and settings, ensuring effective resource allocation and program implementation.
